item.title: Japan's reported outreach push at APEC while refusing to correct mistakes shows insincerity amid Taiwan-related row: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 16:35:00
APEC promotional banners hang from lampposts along a major road in Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong Province, on November 10, 2026. Photo: VCG Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's prospects of holding formal talks with the Chinese leader during the upcoming APEC leaders' meeting in Shenzhen remain uncertain, as Kyodo News reported Tuesday, citing multiple sources familiar with China-Japan relations, that efforts to arrange such a meeting had not achieved progress. The report linked the difficulties to tensions over Takaichi's erroneous remarks on a "Taiwan contingency" in the Japanese Diet in November of 2025. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun on Wednesday addressed a related inquiry. As the host of APEC2026, China is actively fulfilling its responsibilities as host and stands ready to work with all parties to ensure the success of the APEC China Year, Guo said when asked whether Chinese and Japanese leaders would meet on the sidelines of next week's APEC meetings. Guo added that China has made its position on China-Japan relations clear on multiple occasions. A directors' meeting of the Rules and Administration Committee of Japan's House of Representatives on Tuesday approved Takaichi's overseas travel schedule, according to Jiji Press. The report said that Takaichi would visit the Philippines and China from November 16 to 19, attending ASEAN-related summits in the Philippines and the APEC leaders' meeting in China. Kyodo reported that the Japanese government would continue seeking a formal meeting until the last minute, but a handshake or brief encounter between the two leaders during APEC was seen as a more realistic possibility. The report was based on unnamed sources, and the Global Times could not independently verify the claims made by the sources cited in the report. Lian Degui, director of the Center for Japanese Studies at Shanghai International Studies University, told the Global Times on Wednesday that it was unrealistic to expect a formal meeting between the two leaders, at a time when China-Japan relations are at a low point because of Takaichi's erroneous remarks a year ago, given that the Japanese side remains unwilling to correct its mistakes. Lian noted that it was both arrogant and lacking in self-respect for Japan to expect a warm reception while showing disrespect toward China. Earlier, Bloomberg reported Monday, citing people familiar with the matter, that Japanese officials had sought assurances from China that Takaichi would receive the same treatment as other world leaders at APEC, including at least a customary handshake. The sources also said Tokyo would protest any unusual arrangements during the meeting. Lian said Japan's concerns about Takaichi's treatment even before her arrival in China reveal the Japanese side's guilty conscience and contradictory attitude: It is unwilling to correct its mistakes but wants to avoid being snubbed. This also suggests that Japan is seeking to achieve its diplomatic objectives without meeting the prerequisites for improving bilateral relations, the expert said, suggesting a lack of sincerity. Takaichi said Friday that China was an important neighbor and that, despite challenges in bilateral relations, the two countries had built up ties over many years. She claimed Japan would comprehensively advance its strategic relationship of mutual benefit with China, according to Fuji News Network. Her remarks came ahead of the first anniversary of her erroneous remarks related to China's Taiwan region during a session of the Diet in November last year, which have severely undermined China-Japan relations since. Lian further noted that while Japan emphasizes its willingness to engage in dialogue with China, it avoids addressing the need to correct its own mistakes as a prerequisite for such dialogue, attempting to sidestep the issue in an irresponsible manner. Such a continued refusal to reflect on its own actions not only shows disrespect toward others but also damages Japan's own international image. Japan should engage with other countries in good faith and take concrete steps to correct its mistakes, the expert said.

item.title: China's NEV exports hit 606,000 units in October, up 140% year-on-year: CAAM
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 16:13:00
New-energy vehicles are ready for export at the Toumen Port roll-on, roll-off terminal in Linhai, East China's Zhejiang Province, on September 22, 2026. In the first eight months, China's total auto exports reached 7.153 million units, up 66.7 percent year-on-year, according to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers. Photo: VCG China's automobile exports maintained strong momentum in October, with new energy vehicles (NEVs) emerging as a key growth engine amid intensifying competition at home and expanding demand abroad, industry insiders said on Wednesday. The remarks come as the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM) on Wednesday announced that China exported 1.066 million vehicles in October, up 60.2 percent year-on-year. Of that total, NEV exports reached 606,000 units, up 140 percent year-on-year. In the first 10 months of the year, China's cumulative vehicle exports totaled 9.271 million units, including 4.612 million NEVs, whose exports rose 130 percent year-on-year, CAAM data showed. The latest data showed that China's automobile output and sales both exceeded 3 million units in October, rising from the previous month. NEVs continued to gain market share, with output and sales reaching 2.017 million and 1.94 million units respectively, up 13.8 percent and 13.1 percent year-on-year. NEV sales accounted for 64.3 percent of total new vehicle sales in October, CCTV News reported. For the January-October period, NEV sales made up 54.8 percent of China's total vehicle sales, underscoring the sector's growing dominance. In the passenger vehicle segment, NEVs captured more than 70 percent of the domestic market in October, according to CAAM. Industry experts said the rising share of NEVs is not a short-term phenomenon, but the result of technological upgrading, stronger product competitiveness, and growing consumer acceptance. They added that China's EV industry is entering a new phase in which competition is intensifying in an increasingly crowded domestic market, while overseas markets are providing additional growth opportunities. Analysts said China's auto industry is currently facing a "domestic stock competition, overseas incremental breakthrough" pattern: fierce competition in the home market is pushing companies to improve efficiency, lower costs, and accelerate innovation, while exports are becoming a critical outlet for capacity and growth. According to the CAAM data, China's vehicle exports have now exceeded 1 million units for five consecutive months, while NEVs have accounted for more than 50 percent of exports for five straight months. Experts said this export pattern reflects a structural shift in China's auto industry, with NEVs increasingly becoming the main force in global expansion. Chinese automakers are benefiting from competitive pricing, improving technology, and a more complete industrial chain covering batteries, motors, electronic controls, and software systems. "In the domestic market, competition is increasingly centered on product quality, intelligent features, and cost-effectiveness," Wu Songquan, an expert from the China Automotive Technology and Research Center, told the Global Times on Wednesday. "At the same time, overseas markets are offering significant room for expansion as Chinese automakers improve brand recognition and supply chain competitiveness." China's NEV market is expected to remain resilient, supported by continued policy backing, product innovation, and export growth. According to the analyst, policy support has played an important role. China has continued to encourage NEV adoption through measures such as charging infrastructure development, green mobility incentives, and industrial upgrading policies, helping reinforce the sector's foundation. "As China's NEV sector consolidates its position at home and accelerates its push abroad, the industry is increasingly seen as a key pillar of the country's manufacturing upgrade and export competitiveness," Wu said. Global Times

item.title: China firmly backs Cuba in safeguarding rights, interests: Chinese FM
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 15:56:00
CHINA / DIPLOMACY China firmly backs Cuba in safeguarding rights, interests: Chinese FM By Xinhua Published: Nov 11, 2026 03:56 PM Updated: Nov 11, 2026 07:59 PM
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi held talks with Cuban Minister of Foreign Affairs Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla in Beijing on Wednesday. Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said that the world is facing unprecedented changes in a century, and no matter how the situation evolves, China will firmly support Cuba in safeguarding its national sovereignty and legitimate rights and interests, and in opposing sanctions, blockades and external interference. China stands ready to work with Cuba to deliver on the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, and continuously consolidate and develop the friendly relations between China and Cuba, Wang said. Wang said China is willing to strengthen communication and coordination with Cuba in multilateral fields, continue to support and cooperate with each other on multilateral platforms, and jointly oppose power politics and unilateral acts. Rodriguez said Cuba appreciates China's support and consistently adheres firmly to the one-China principle, opposing interference in China's internal affairs by any external forces. Noting that China plays an important role in safeguarding world peace, championing multilateralism and building a more democratic international order, Rodriguez said Cuba and China share common ground and broad consensus on international and regional issues. Cuba supports the vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity and the four global initiatives put forward by China, stands ready to further strengthen coordination with China in multilateral areas and deliver more cooperation outcomes.

item.title: China looks to advance CAFTA 3.0 upgrade protocol, deepen cooperation with ASEAN at upcoming summit: FM
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 15:49:00
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun Asked about China's expectations for the 29th China-ASEAN Summit, to be held in Manila, the Philippines, from November 15 to 16, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Wednesday that China looks forward to using this meeting to enhance solidarity and mutual trust with ASEAN, build consensus on cooperation, and promote the early entry into force of the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area (CAFTA) 3.0 Upgrade Protocol. China also looks forward to using the meeting to deepen cooperation in areas such as AI, the digital economy, energy security, connectivity, and poverty reduction and development, and work together to build a peaceful, tranquil, prosperous, beautiful and friendly shared home, so as to inject more stability and certainty into regional peace and development, Guo said at a regular press conference. This year marks the fifth anniversary of the establishment of the China-ASEAN comprehensive strategic partnership. Over the past five years, under the joint guidance of leaders from both sides, China-ASEAN cooperation has flourished and yielded fruitful results, consistently remaining at the forefront of regional cooperation, Guo said. "The cooperation has not only benefited both sides and their peoples but also made important contributions to regional peace, stability and prosperity," the spokesperson said. Currently, the world has entered a new period of turbulence and transformation, and the greatest aspiration of people in the region is to seek peace, pursue development and promote prosperity, Guo noted. Global Times

item.title: Taiwan question brooks no external interference: mainland spokesperson on question about China-US discussions at APEC
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 12:20:00
Taiwan Affairs Office spokesperson Zhang Han When asked about discussions between China and the US on Taiwan-related issues during the APEC meetings, Zhang Han, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said on Wednesday that the Taiwan question is purely China's internal affair, which brooks no external interference. Zhang stressed that peace and stability across the Taiwan Straits can only be guaranteed by unequivocally opposing "Taiwan independence” and firmly upholding the one-China principle. Taiwan is part of China, and the one-China principle and the three China-US joint communiqués form the political foundation of China-US relations, the spokesperson noted. The Democratic Progressive Party authorities' attempts to seek “Taiwan independence” by relying on external forces will only turn Taiwan into a pawn in the hands of external forces, ultimately leaving it with no escape from the fate of being abandoned, Zhang said. Global Times

item.title: Lithuania's political gamble comes at too high a price: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 00:34:00
Lithuania Illustration: Chen Xia/GT Recently, media reports said Lithuania's foreign affairs department is pushing to change the name of the "Taiwan Representative Office." Since the beginning of this year, Lithuania has been floating signals about "restoring diplomatic relations with China." Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda has acknowledged that setting up the "Taiwan Representative Office" was a mistake, and the new government has set a goal of normalizing diplomatic relations with China. But beyond that, we have so far not seen more concrete steps from Lithuania to improve the situation. Five years ago, Lithuania's previous government crossed China's red line on the Taiwan question. Disregarding China's solemn protests, it openly allowed the Taiwan authorities to establish a so-called representative office under the name "Taiwan," deliberately creating the false impression of "one China, one Taiwan." This move seriously undermined the political foundation of China-Lithuania relations and made Lithuania an outlier among EU member states in their relations with China. Yet Vilnius gravely underestimated China's capacity for strategic countermeasures. Before bilateral relations deteriorated in 2021, practical economic and trade cooperation had kept bilateral trade on an upward trend for an extended period, reaching a historic high in 2020. Following the deterioration of relations, however, economic and trade cooperation suffered a comprehensive downturn. The harsh realities of the past five years have demonstrated that abandoning the one-China principle and openly supporting the Taiwan authorities haven't benefited Lithuania. Instead, they have damaged its economy and left it diplomatically disadvantaged. Clearly, Lithuania's current government is unwilling to continue shouldering the burden of this disastrous legacy. Yet it remains hesitant and indecisive when it comes to addressing the fundamental issue of correcting its mistakes. For example, while signaling its hope to "put bilateral relations back on track," it has simultaneously claimed that it is "too early" to discuss renaming the so-called "Taiwan Representative Office." To some extent, the current government's hope to mend ties with China has been driven by Lithuania's difficult domestic economic situation and public opinion. A Lithuanian survey conducted this year shows that nearly 60 percent of Lithuanians have recognized the illusory nature and enormous costs of attempting to "use Taiwan to contain China," and want their government to repair relations with China and abandon opportunistic political maneuvering. However, Vilnius still clings to illusions about the empty promises made by certain Western actors and the flattering labels of "democracy" they have bestowed upon it. That is why Lithuania continues to hold on to this political hot potato, despite the discomfort it causes. This also suggests that Lithuania may not yet be prepared for the normalization of relations with China. The one-China principle is a widely recognized norm governing international relations and a broad consensus of the international community. It also constitutes the political foundation of China-Lithuania and China-EU relations. Anti-China forces in the West have sought to turn Lithuania into a strategic pawn in their geopolitical maneuvering, encouraging it to play the "Taiwan card" to provoke China. Such underhanded tactics, which tie the interests of smaller countries to great-power rivalry for the benefits of others, will ultimately leave those smaller countries bearing the consequences and suffering a backlash. Lithuania's prolonged and costly detour has made this reality even clearer to the international community. It must be noted that renaming the Taiwan-related representative office is an inevitable trend, and such a change would be only the first step, not the final destination, in Lithuania's efforts to correct its mistakes. Even if Lithuania changes the erroneous name of the so-called "Taiwan Representative Office," this would not mean that its relations with China could immediately "return to the past." Nor should Vilnius attempt to use the proposed name change as a bargaining chip in negotiations with China. The Taiwan question is China's internal affair and the core of China's core interests. There is no room for compromise or concession. What Lithuania needs to do is bring its foreign policy fully into alignment with the one-China principle. Only then can bilateral relations potentially resume practical cooperation, and only then can Lithuania truly move beyond its past strategic dilemma. The one-China principle is a binding constraint, not an optional choice. Any separatist attempt to play the "Taiwan card" or engage in word games over names will inevitably run up against the solid wall of the one-China principle. The higher one jumps, the harder the impact. All parties should have a clear understanding of this reality: Any attempt to play the "Taiwan card" for opportunistic political gains or engage in political gambling is doomed to fail. China is open to communication, but Lithuania must also demonstrate the right attitude toward dialogue. We hope Lithuania will correct its mistakes as soon as possible, honor the political commitments it made in the communiqué on the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries, and return to the right path of adhering to the one-China principle. It should translate its stated willingness to improve bilateral relations into concrete actions, thereby creating the conditions for the normalization of China-Lithuania relations. In particular, certain Lithuanian politicians should refrain from political opportunism on this fundamental matter of principle. Otherwise, no matter how many signals they send expressing a "desire to restore relations," such statements will amount to nothing more than empty gestures.

item.title: Manila becomes a testing ground for Japan to break through postwar defense constraints
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 23:11:00
Japan, the Philippines Illustration: Liu Xiangya/GT The Philippines has emerged as the latest testing ground for Japan's attempts to extend its military network overseas under the guise of "security aid." According to Japanese and Philippine media reports, Japan on Monday agreed to provide radar systems to the Philippine Navy and surveillance and reconnaissance drones to its air force, which is worth 4.3 billion yen ($27.2 million), representing Japan's largest Official Security Assistance (OSA) grant to date. Jiji Press reported that this marks the first transfer of a complete defense equipment system under the framework. Previously, assistance was limited to dual-use products and parts. It is also reported that Tokyo is considering replicating this practice to other countries. From dual-use components to complete defense systems, the boundaries governing Japan's overseas transfers of military equipment are being pushed back. Wang Qiang, a Chinese military expert, noted that Japan's provision of radar systems and drones to the Philippines is a significant departure from its "exclusively defense-oriented" policy, potentially paving the way for the future transfer of lethal weapons. This is not an isolated assistance project, but part of Japan's broader efforts to break through its postwar defense constraints and expand its military capabilities. In recent years, Japan has accelerated the development of offensive weapons and revised limits on defense equipment exports, while loudly advocating for the building of bilateral and multilateral security networks with so-called "like-minded countries." By leveraging the US alliance network in the Asia-pacific region, Japan seeks to rally partners, strengthen military coordination, elevate its position in the regional security architecture and extend its military influence. The Philippines, both a US treaty ally and a long-standing economic partner of Japan, has naturally become an ideal foothold for this strategy. As part of Tokyo's broader strategic push, defense cooperation between Japan and the Philippines is deepening. The two countries have reportedly agreed to begin talks on a deal that would allow Tokyo to provide used destroyers to Manila's navy. What is presented as security cooperation is increasingly becoming a convenient channel for Japan to loosen its postwar military constraints and re-establish an overseas military presence. The greater concern lies in the wider military network Japan is seeking to build through these equipment provisions. Wang noted that Japan occupies a key position at the northern end of the First Island Chain, while the Philippines is an important strategic foothold at its southern end. By supplying radar systems and drones, Japan is helping the Philippines strengthen its maritime and aerial surveillance and intelligence-gathering capabilities, while facilitating the integration of relevant information into Japan's and potentially the US military's intelligence networks in the western Pacific. This could potentially strengthen surveillance of Chinese naval and air activities. In other words, Japan is not simply supplying a few pieces of equipment; it is using partner countries to construct a more targeted regional military cooperation network. The expansion of this military network is hardly a recipe for greater regional security. Japan repeatedly claims to be safeguarding regional peace, yet its actions involve drawing countries into closer military alignment and introducing new variables into an already sensitive security environment. What gives a country that continues to export military equipment and build military networks the right to present itself as a guardian of regional stability? Lü Chao, a Chinese expert on Northeast Asian affairs at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times that Japan used Official Development Assistance (ODA) to support the economic and social development of neighboring developing countries in the past. Today, however, Japan is increasingly using OSA to export defense equipment overseas. The name on the aid package has changed, but the logic of Japan's military expansion is becoming increasingly apparent. Established in 2023, OSA provides a new vehicle for Japan to give its militarist legacy a fresh overseas foothold under the guise of security cooperation, pushing the Asia-Pacific further toward military tensions. Today's "first" could soon become tomorrow's precedent. If Japan's defense transfers begin with radar systems and drones, what might come next under the guise of "security assistance"? When a country repeatedly repackages the dismantling of its postwar constraints as "policy innovation" and dresses up military expansion as a contribution to regional stability, the international community has little reason to continue giving it the benefit of the doubt.

item.title: GT Voice: India should embrace advanced clean tech to curb air pollution
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 21:24:00
Early morning smog engulfs the capital city after Diwali celebrations, on November 9, 2026 in New Delhi, India. Photo: VCG The Diwali fireworks have faded, but the smog over New Delhi has lingered. On Sunday, India's capital recorded a 24-hour average Air Quality Index (AQI) of 376, its worst Diwali-day reading since 2021. On Tuesday morning, the AQI hovered above 300, remaining in the "very poor" category. Authorities imposed emergency curbs on certain construction activities and older, more polluting vehicles before the festival. To blame the air crisis on fireworks alone would be missing the larger picture. Nearly every autumn and winter in recent years, emissions from automobile vehicles, factories and crop burning combine with construction dust and stagnant weather to blanket northern India in smog. Diwali is just a flashpoint in a much longer-running problem. The deeper question is why severe air pollution remains such a persistent challenge for a country making strides in renewable energy. Part of the answer lies in the difficulty of turning the expansion of clean power into a broader shift away from fossil fuels and other sources of pollution. India's solar expansion has been substantial. Installed capacity grew 38.8 percent to 135.81 gigawatts in 2025. Yet coal still accounted for about 71 percent of the country's electricity source last year, according to the International Energy Agency. That share was down from 74 percent in 2024, a sign of progress, but also a measure of how much conventional power India continues to rely on. Solar power depends on sunlight, but factories and households need reliable power around the clock. Energy storage facilities and stronger grids are essential if rising renewable capacity is to displace more coal in India. Rising electricity demand makes the transition even harder. In the first 10 months of the 2025-26 fiscal year, India added 8,810 megawatts of coal-fired capacity. For a fast-growing economy, maintaining reliable energy supply while changing its energy mix is a formidable task. China's experience offers a useful perspective, though the two countries face different conditions. Between 2013 and 2022, China's PM2.5 concentration fell 57 percent while its GDP expanded by 69 percent. Here, stricter enforcement of environmental protection measures and revamping a country's old industrial structure are of great importance. And, replacing coal-fired heating requires cleaner equipment and supporting infrastructure. Cutting vehicle emissions call for electric transportation and fast-charging networks, while tackling crop-residue burning needs machinery to collect and process agricultural waste. Making these alternatives widely available and affordable depended on manufacturing capacity, reliable supply chain and sustained investment. For India, taking emergency measures may ease severe pollution, but restrictions on construction and transportation would produce economic costs. Lasting improvements in air quality require cleaner, affordable alternatives that businesses and households could adopt, particularly as industrialization and urbanization continue. The question is how India can accelerate this transition while strengthening its manufacturing base. India has made domestic solar manufacturing a priority. Its Approved List of Models and Manufacturers framework is to extend to solar ingots and wafers from June 2028. However, in September 2025, Indian trade authorities recommended imposing anti-dumping duties on certain Chinese solar cells. Although domestic manufacturing tends to create jobs and build resilience, restrictive measures on imports would make clean-energy equipment scarcer and more costly, eventually slowing new energy transition. India should not turn its back on advanced clean technology and clean gears. This is where international cooperation could play a constructive role. China's manufacturing expertise in making batteries, electric vehicles and power storage facilities is of great help for India, which aspires to curb atmospheric pollution. As a matter of fact, China- developed clean technologies and products are welcomed by many countries in the world. In the first nine months of 2026, China's electric vehicle exports rose 72.3 percent year-on-year, lithium battery exports climbed 36.4 percent and exports of wind turbines and their components increased 22.4 percent, according to the Chinese customs authorities. The opportunities are concrete: electric two- and three-wheelers could be assembled in India, while solar and storage systems could support Indian factories, and better irrigation and crop-residue equipment could serve rural communities there. Joint ventures, component sourcing and technology partnerships could create new business opportunities for Indian businesses. Such cooperation could also help Indian companies build expertise in manufacturing, engineering, maintenance and distribution, which will also strengthen India's participation in global supply chains while supporting India's pursuit of greater industrial self-reliance. The smog is a reminder that progress in renewable energy cannot be measured by installed capacity alone. The real test is whether cleaner technologies can deliver meaningful improvements in factories, on city streets and in people's daily lives. For India, greater openness to international industrial and trade cooperation could help accelerate the new-energy transition and clean the nation's polluted air.

item.title: Kuaizhou targets 2027 maiden flight and first-stage recovery of reusable rocket, unveils development roadmap
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 19:39:00
Kuaizhou rocket model Photo: VCG China's space sector has made further progress in the development of a new reusable launch vehicle, with Wuhan-based Kuaizhou Aerospace targeting 2027 for the maiden orbital flight and first-stage recovery of its Kuaizhou-6 liquid-propellant rocket, which is designed to carry a payload of about 20 tons. The company also plans to conduct at least 50 launches over the next three years using its Kuaizhou-1A and Kuaizhou-11 rockets, the Global Times learned from Kuaizhou Aerospace on Tuesday. According to a press release by the firm, Kuaizhou will accelerate development of its Kuaizhou-6 reusable liquid-propellant rocket, targeting its maiden orbital flight and first-stage recovery in 2027. The rocket is designed to have a payload capacity of about 20 tons. By the middle of the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), the company plans to upgrade the rocket with a 140-ton-class liquid-propellant engine and put it into large-scale commercial service, further increasing its payload capacity and advancing the engineering application of reusable launch technology. The company also plans to develop lower-cost medium-lift launch vehicles. Building on its existing technologies and production capacity, it will adopt a standardized, modular and flexible approach to developing the Kuaizhou-12 solid-liquid hybrid rocket. The rocket, with a payload capacity of about 10 tons, is scheduled to make its maiden flight and enter the market in 2027, with a targeted launch cost of no more than 20,000 yuan ($2,800) per kilogram. Kuaizhou also outlined a three-stage roadmap for its liquid-propellant engine program. In 2027, it aims to complete a cumulative 15,000 seconds of hot-fire testing for its 80-ton-class liquid oxygen-methane engine and deliver the engine for operational use, while completing design-validation hot-fire tests of a 140-ton-class engine. Before 2030, the company plans to complete design-validation hot-fire tests of a 200- to 300-ton-class liquid oxygen-methane engine. Meanwhile, Kuaizhou plans to conduct more than 50 launches over the next three years using its Kuaizhou-1A and Kuaizhou-11 carrier rockets, aiming to establish routine, high-frequency launch operations. The company said the effort would help consolidate its rapid space-response capabilities and support national emergency needs. To further expand its ambitions, Kuaizhou plans to strengthen its research, testing and final assembly facilities at its Wuhan headquarters, while further developing its liquid-propulsion research and development center in Beijing. The company also plans to expand its testing capabilities for 300-ton-class liquid-propellant engines and establish testing and launch capabilities in Jiuquan and Wenchang, aiming to achieve independent control over the entire chain of research, development, production and testing.

item.title: Man held for damaging government service center building with construction machinery in Shaanxi: police
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 17:41:00
The government service center building damaged by an excavator Photo: Screenshot from media reports A person has been placed under criminal compulsory measures for allegedly damaging a building with construction machinery at a government service center in Northwest China's Shaanxi Province. The incident occurred at around 11 am Monday. The suspect, surnamed Hu, 47, was brought under control by police at the scene, and no injuries were reported, according to a notice released by Xi'an public security bureau on its official WeChat account. The government service center resumed operations on Monday afternoon, the notice said. Hu has since been placed under criminal compulsory measures, and the case is under further investigation, according to the notice. Global Times
